title: X Rays: Atomic Origins and Applications
lead: X rays come from the anode of an x-ray tube in two ways: as braking radiation from electrons that slow down, and as characteristic x rays from atoms whose inner shells are emptied and refilled. Their high photon energies let them pass through matter to make medical images, and their short wavelengths let them reveal how the atoms of a crystal are arranged.
objectives: Define x-ray tube and its spectrum.
Specify the use of x rays in medical observations.
Explain the use of x rays in CT scanners in diagnostics.
summary_html:
• X rays are relatively high-frequency EM radiation. They are produced by transitions between inner-shell electron levels, which produce x rays characteristic of the atomic element, or by decelerating electrons.
  • X rays have many uses, including medical diagnostics and x-ray diffraction.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 30.20) X-ray spectrum obtained when energetic electrons strike a material, such as in the anode of a CRT. The smooth part of the spectrum is bremsstrahlung radiation, while the peaks are characteristic of the anode material. A different anode material would have characteristic x-ray peaks at different frequencies. (Figure 30.21) A characteristic x ray is emitted when an electron fills an inner-shell vacancy, as shown for several transitions in this approximate energy level diagram for a multiple-electron atom. Characteristic x rays are labeled according to the shell that had the vacancy and the shell from which the electron came. A Kα x ray, for example, is produced when an electron coming from the n = 2 shell fills the n = 1 shell vacancy.

exercises.prompt: Explain why characteristic x rays are the most energetic in the EM emission spectrum of a given element.

answer.solution: Characteristic x rays are emitted when an electron fills a vacancy in an inner shell, the K or L shell. Inner-shell electrons are close to the nucleus and feel nearly its whole charge, so they are bound far more tightly than the outer electrons whose transitions give the visible and ultraviolet lines. The photon carries the difference between two of these deeply bound levels, thousands of electron volts in a heavy atom, so it is the most energetic photon the atom emits.

exercises.prompt: Why does the energy of characteristic x rays become increasingly greater for heavier atoms?

answer.solution: The inner-shell levels are roughly hydrogen-like with an effective charge $Z - 1$, so their energies are about $\kEn = -(Z - 1)^2\kEobohr/n^2$. A characteristic x ray carries the difference between two such levels, which grows approximately as $Z^2$. A heavier atom has more charge in its nucleus, binds its inner electrons more tightly, and so emits more energetic characteristic x rays.

exercises.prompt: Observers at a safe distance from an atmospheric test of a nuclear bomb feel its heat but receive none of its copious x rays. Why is air opaque to x rays but transparent to infrared?

answer.solution: An x-ray photon carries thousands of electron volts, far more than is needed to ionize the nitrogen and oxygen of the air, so x rays are absorbed and scattered all along their path. Over the kilometers between the bomb and a safe observer, the air in the way is a great deal of matter, and almost none of the x rays get through. An infrared photon carries only a fraction of an electron volt, too little to ionize the air or excite the electrons of its molecules, and nitrogen and oxygen absorb little infrared, so it travels through the air with little loss.

exercises.prompt: Crystal lattices can be examined with x rays but not UV. Why?

answer.solution: A structure diffracts a wave strongly only when its spacing is comparable to the wavelength. The atoms of a crystal are about $0.1\;\text{nm}$ apart. X rays have wavelengths of about $0.01$ to $0.1\;\text{nm}$, so a lattice diffracts them into a pattern that reveals its arrangement, while ultraviolet has wavelengths of tens to hundreds of nanometers, hundreds of times the spacing, and the lattice gives it no useful pattern.

exercises.prompt: CT scanners do not detect details smaller than about 0.5 mm. Is this limitation due to the wavelength of x rays? Explain.

answer.solution: No. Medical x rays have wavelengths of about $0.01\;\text{nm}$, millions of times smaller than $0.5\;\text{mm}$, so diffraction sets no limit near that size; x rays cast sharp shadows of objects as small as teeth and far smaller. The limit comes from the scanner and the patient: the size and spacing of the detectors, the width of the beam, the number of directions measured, and the number of x-ray photons that can be used without giving too large a dose.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the shortest-wavelength x-ray radiation that can be generated in an x-ray tube with an applied voltage of 50.0 kV? (b) Calculate the photon energy in eV. (c) Explain the relationship of the photon energy to the applied voltage.

parts.hint: The shortest wavelength belongs to the most energetic photon, $\kEmax = \kqe\kV$; then $\klam = h\kc/\kEmax$ with $h\kc = 1240\;\text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}$.
An electron accelerated through 50.0 kV gains 50.0 keV, and the most energetic photon takes all of it.

answer.solution:
(a) $0.248\times 10^{-10}\;\text{m}$
(b) 50.0 keV
(c) The photon energy is simply the applied voltage times the electron charge, so the value of the voltage in volts is the same as the value of the energy in electron volts.

exercises.prompt: An x ray tube has an applied voltage of 100 kV. (a) What is the most energetic x-ray photon it can produce? Express your answer in electron volts and joules. (b) Find the wavelength of such an X–ray.

parts.hint: Use $\kEmax = \kqe\kV$: an electron accelerated through 100 kV gains 100 keV.
Multiply the energy in eV by $1.60\times 10^{-19}\;\text{J/eV}$.

exercises.prompt: What are the approximate energies of the $K_{\alpha}$ and $K_{\beta}$ x rays for copper?

parts.part: (a) the energy of the $K_{\alpha}$ x ray
parts.hint: Copper has $Z = 29$. As in Example 30.3, use hydrogen-like levels with an effective charge $Z - 1 = 28$ and find $E_2 - E_1$.

parts.part: (b) the energy of the $K_{\beta}$ x ray
parts.hint: A $K_{\beta}$ x ray comes from the $n = 3$ to $n = 1$ transition, so find $E_3 - E_1$ with the same effective charge.

exercises.prompt: Unreasonable Results. (a) What voltage must be applied to an X-ray tube to obtain 0.0100-fm-wavelength X-rays for use in exploring the details of nuclei? (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) Which assumptions are unreasonable or inconsistent?

answer.hint: Find the photon energy from $\kEmax = h\kc/\klam$ with $h\kc = 1240\;\text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}$ and $1\;\text{fm} = 10^{-6}\;\text{nm}$; an electron needs a voltage of as many volts as the photon has electron volts.
answer.solution:
(a) $1.24\times 10^{11}\;\text{V}$
(b) The voltage is extremely large compared with any practical value.
(c) The assumption of such a short wavelength by this method is unreasonable.
